source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Principles of metareasoning / Do the Right Thing
finding: Founding theory. A computation is an action. Its value is the expected gain in decision quality it brings, minus its time cost. Think only while some computation has positive net value; then act.
numbers: Not opened this session. Details taken from how later papers (a02, a03, a05) describe it. Formal VOC: expected over new belief of best-action value, minus best-action value now, minus cost (eq 1 in a11).
limits: Original text not read; its own experiments (game-search algorithms of 1989-91) not checked. Assumes an additive cost of time (Harada 1997 gives conditions, per a02). The DOI is from memory.
agent_relevance: This is the base of our S0 gate and S6 trigger: spend a step only if its expected gain beats its cost.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Formalises the metalevel decision problem as a belief-state MDP. States are sequences of computation outcomes; each computation costs c; stopping pays the best posterior mean. Traces the idea to Matheson 1968 and Howard's value of information, then Dean-Boddy, Horvitz 1987, Russell-Wefald 1988/91.
numbers: Theorem 5: expected number of computations of the optimal policy is at most VPI/c. Theorem 10: the one-armed Bernoulli problem needs at most (1-mu)/c - 3, at most 1/(4c) - 3, computations. Theorem 7: if the myopic policy computes, so does the optimal policy.
quote: The metalevel decision problem can itself be formulated and solved decision-theoretically
limits: Theory for independent-action selection problems; cost of computation taken as fixed per step.
agent_relevance: The VPI/c bound gives a principled cap on thinking steps. A plain code counter can use it as a stop rule.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Myopic VOC (Russell-Wefald single-step greedy) stops too early: it quits as soon as no single computation can change the chosen action. The blinkered policy fixes this by looking at many computations on one action at a time. It costs time linear in the number of arms.
numbers: Fig 2: 25-arm Bernoulli problem, 1000 trials, regret = (best utility - chosen utility) + c*n. Blinkered policy significantly beats myopic, UCB1 variants and ESP. Myopic regret plateaus because it reaches states where no single computation flips the choice.
quote: The myopic policy is an extreme approximation, often stopping far too early.
limits: Needs independent actions (subtree independence). Plain Bernoulli samples, not LLM thoughts.
agent_relevance: Warning for S0/S6: a one-step gain test under-thinks when one step cannot change the answer but five steps could. Use multi-step lookahead or a floor.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Bandit algorithms such as UCB1 do not solve the Russell-Wefald metalevel problem. Bandits count reward during sampling and never stop; selection problems pay only for the final choice and have a stopping rule. Bandit rules also under-explore low-estimate arms. A hybrid (VOI at the root, UCT below) was tested in Go.
numbers: Go (Pachi engine, 9x9, 1000 repeats per setting, 5k-15k simulations per move): with stopping threshold c = 1e-6 the VOI policy almost always beat plain UCT and reached a 64% win rate at 10000 samples per move. Gain largest at intermediate sample counts; at very low counts early stopping hurts.
quote: One consequence of the mismatch is that bandit policies are inappropriately biased away from exploring actions whose current utility estimates are low.
limits: One engine, one board size. Win rate is read from the text; no confidence interval given. Effect shrinks at very low or very high sample budgets.
agent_relevance: Explicit value-based stopping beat a fixed search rule with the same engine in a real game. Supports a cost-aware stop over a fixed budget.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations
finding: Bayesian metalevel policy search (BMPS) makes VOC tractable. It approximates VOC as a weighted mix of three features: myopic VOI, perfect-information value (VPI) and cost. Weights are learned by Bayesian optimisation. Claimed to be the first domain-general learner of how to metareason.
numbers: Regression: the three features explain 90.8% to 100% of the variance in exact VOC (cost 0.001 to 0.1). Weights shift from 0.76 VPI + 0.46 VOI1 - 4.5 cost to 0.00 VPI + 1.00 VOI1 - 1.00 cost as cost rises. Binary prediction task: BMPS at most 5.19% below optimal; 20.3% better than meta-greedy on average.
limits: Toy problems, simulation only. Authors say metareasoning pays only when object-level computation is much costlier than metareasoning itself.
agent_relevance: At low cost the one-step test is not enough; the VPI term matters. At high cost one-step VOI minus cost is enough. This sets when a simple S0 gate is safe.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations
finding: Bernoulli metalevel problem (choose among options): BMPS is near optimal and beats meta-greedy, full deliberation and a DQN.
numbers: BMPS 0.6535 vs optimal 0.6596 (99.1% of optimal, t(1998) = -7.43), meta-greedy 0.60, DQN 0.58, full deliberation 0.20. Blinkered 0.6559 (BMPS differs by 0.37%). 2000 test episodes. BMPS beat meta-greedy for cost below 0.03.
limits: Simulated agents only.
agent_relevance: Full deliberation scored 0.20 vs 0.65 for selective thinking. Thinking on everything is the worst policy once thought has a price.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations
finding: Bernoulli metalevel tree (planning): BMPS reaches 98.4% of optimal at tree heights 2-3 and beats meta-greedy, recursively blinkered and full deliberation overall. A tornado-evacuation example (k = 10 or 30 cities, T = 24 h) beats uniform allocation of simulations.
numbers: Planning: BMPS 0.392 reward per object-level action vs meta-greedy 0.307, recursively blinkered 0.368, full deliberation -1.740 (all p below 1e-15). On h in {2,3}: optimal 0.373 vs BMPS 0.367. Advantage over meta-greedy largest when computation is cheap and grows with tree height.
limits: The tornado scenario is hypothetical. Offline training of BMPS is a cost that only pays back if the problem repeats.
agent_relevance: Full deliberation can be strongly negative once thinking has a price. Argues for a learned trigger over a fixed schedule (G1).

source: Lin, Kolobov, Kamar, Horvitz (2015) Metareasoning for Planning Under Uncertainty
finding: Metareasoning for MDP planning is itself an MDP (meta-MDP) over the world state plus the solver's internal state. Optimal metareasoning is only polynomially harder than solving the base MDP (P-complete) but still impractical. Gives a cheap VOC approximation using Bounded RTDP value bounds, time linear in the number of actions per visited state.
numbers: Theorem 2: meta-MDP time is polynomial in solver time. Theorem 3: P-complete under NC-reduction. Experiments: four domains, each run 1000 times to goal, 50-action BRTDP trajectories.
quote: Metareasoning for SSP MDPs is P-complete under N C-reduction.
limits: Heuristic VOC from bounds. Gains depend on the metareasoning gap (cost of the heuristic policy over cost of the optimal policy); in an adversarial domain (DynamicNOP-1) gains are small.
agent_relevance: The meta-metareasoning problem: deciding costs thinking. The gate must be cheaper than the thought it gates. Predict whether a gate pays from the size of the gap.

source: Lin, Kolobov, Kamar, Horvitz (2015) Metareasoning for Planning Under Uncertainty
finding: Baseline results. A fixed think-then-act baseline (ThinkAct) fails where thinking at the start is costly (Traps domain); a think-with-probability baseline does well only when its parameter is tuned to the cost ratio. The VOC metareasoner adapts without tuning.
numbers: Domains: Stochastic (vary think/act costs), Traps, DynamicNOP-1 (adversarial), DynamicNOP-2. With low think cost or high act cost, baselines with large n or p do well; otherwise the metareasoner wins. Exact values are in figures that were not extracted.
limits: Only text claims recorded.
agent_relevance: A fixed schedule (always think N steps) is right only for one cost ratio. Matches G1 (no scheduled doubt).

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: RaM: reward = log pi(y|z,x) - log pi(y|x) - lambda * tokens, i.e. VOC with token count as cost, used inside Expert Iteration (best chain per question kept when advantage is above 0; K = 4 chains, 5 iterations, lambda = 0.1). Trains Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B on ARC, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, ProofWriter (1024 training items each).
numbers: Abstract: 23-45% fewer tokens across three models while accuracy is kept or improved. Text: 35-42% fewer tokens than few-shot CoT and 23-32% fewer than STaR. Per-dataset tables are images and were not extracted.
quote: reducing inference costs (23-45% fewer tokens generated across three models) while maintaining or increasing task performance
limits: Preprint under review. Small base models, closed-answer benchmarks, greedy decoding. No agent or tool-use test (authors list this as a limitation). Needs fine-tuning, so cannot be used as is on a scaffold.
agent_relevance: The VOC reward can be turned into a prompt-level rule: keep a thought only if it raised the answer's probability by more than its token cost.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Adaptivity test: split test items by whether direct few-shot answering was right (easy) or wrong (hard). All methods write fewer tokens on easy items. RaM widens the gap most. The instruct model barely adapts its length to difficulty.
numbers: RaM hard-vs-easy length reduction up to 50.3% on Llama-3.2-3B. Out of distribution on MMLU-CF: RaM writes 28% to 36% fewer output tokens than STaR at similar accuracy. Fact-recall subjects shrank most; physics and engineering shrank least.
limits: Easy/hard is defined by one few-shot direct answer, which is noisy. MMLU-CF is multiple choice.
agent_relevance: A cheap direct-answer attempt can be the probe for 'does this need thought' (S0). Direct-first matches how RaM defines easy.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models
finding: The paper ties its result to a cited meta-analysis (Sprague et al. 2024, over 100 papers): explicit chains help mainly on maths and logic, marginally elsewhere. It also cites work that reasoning where it is unneeded can hurt performance.
numbers: Direct few-shot was poor on GSM8K and ProofWriter, the reasoning-heavy sets; chains gave marginal gains on the others.
limits: Second-hand: claims about Sprague et al. and Liu et al. 2024 come from this paper's text only.
agent_relevance: Supports the gate: for fact-recall items, skip long thinking.

source: Arora and Zanette (2025) Training Language Models to Reason Efficiently
finding: RL with a length penalty on correct responses only, scaled against other correct samples for the same prompt. One hyperparameter alpha traces a cost-accuracy curve. Tested on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B and 7B.
numbers: 7B: 50% fewer tokens with under 5% accuracy loss. By task: GSM8K up to 65% fewer tokens (-1.7 points), MATH500 up to 37% (-2.2), AIME 2024 16% (-3.3). At alpha = 0.2: MATH 4000 to 2600 tokens (-36%, -2.2 points); AIME 13,000 to 9,000 (-27%, -4%). Online RL beat SFT and DPO at equal token use.
quote: reduce compute significantly with minimal loss in performance
limits: Maths only. Savings shrink as problems get harder, which is the VOC-consistent pattern. Training needed.
agent_relevance: Savings are biggest on easy items and smallest on hard ones; a good S0 gate should look the same.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Names overthinking: o1-like models spend many tokens on extra solutions after the first correct one. Defines outcome efficiency (share of tokens that reach the first correct answer) and a process efficiency metric. Mitigates with self-training (SimPO best) on shortened solutions.
numbers: Example: for '2 plus 3' the first correct solution used 39 of 901 tokens, outcome efficiency 4.3%. On MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview, tokens cut 48.6% at the same accuracy; SimPO alone cut 22.3%. Also tested GSM8K, GPQA, AIME.
quote: later solutions marginally contribute to improvements in accuracy
limits: Model family limited (QwQ, R1-style). First-correct-only trimming hurt on hard MATH500 items that need reflection. Efficiency is judged against a known correct answer, which an agent does not have.
agent_relevance: Later rounds rarely raise accuracy on easy items; a stop rule after the first verified answer saves most tokens. Verification must be code (G3).

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating it per prompt ('compute-optimal') is the metareasoning idea in practice.
numbers: More than 4x efficiency gain over best-of-N at equal accuracy (revisions and search). FLOPs-matched: where a smaller model has non-trivial success, test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model; on the hardest questions more pretraining wins.
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate, which itself costs compute. Maths. Gains on the hardest tier are small.
agent_relevance: Gives the boundary: extra thinking does not pay on the hardest items. S6 should not escalate forever.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: A stopping rule for self-consistency: after each sample, stop if a Beta posterior says the leading answer is almost surely ahead of the runner-up. This is optimal stopping with a confidence threshold.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: sample budget cut up to 7.9x, average accuracy drop below 0.1%. Average over reasoning categories 3.3x fewer samples with 0.04% drop; Vicuna-13B 1.9x, GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4x fewer samples.
quote: reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Assumes samples are independent; same-model samples are correlated (our G4), so the stop can be over-confident. Uses only the top two answers.
agent_relevance: A code-side stop rule on agreement is the cheapest S6/stop mechanism, with the G4 caveat that agreement is only a hint.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: Trains R1-distilled models to choose between thinking and NoThinking per problem by RL, with a constraint that accuracy must not fall. Shows NoThinking is better on simple tasks.
numbers: 1.5B and 7B: average response length cut 53.0% and 40.1% on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24 while average accuracy rose 2.4% and 2.3%.
limits: Maths only; needs RL. Difficulty sense is learned from training data.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a skip-thinking gate can raise accuracy, not only save tokens.

source: Fang, Ma, Wang (2025) Thinkless: LLM Learns When to Think
finding: Decoupled GRPO trains one model to emit a control token choosing short or long reasoning, then answer.
numbers: Reduces long-chain use by 50% to 90% on Minerva Algebra, MATH-500, GSM8K (abstract). Other numbers not extracted.
limits: Only abstract-level numbers recorded. Maths.
agent_relevance: Another trained S0 gate; the mode choice is one decision up front.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control
finding: Learned Value of Control (LVOC): people learn by RL to predict the value of control signals (type and intensity) from stimulus features, then pick the signal with best value minus effort cost. Predicts learning and transfer in one visual attention experiment and four Stroop/Flanker experiments.
numbers: On one reanalysed dataset LVOC beat Rescorla-Wagner and Win-Stay-Lose-Shift: BIC LVOC 1817.8, RW 9763.2, WSLS 3449.9 (lower is better), with no parameters fitted to that data. Participant counts not extracted.
limits: Small lab tasks; the BIC comparison is for one dataset only. Other experiments' fit numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Control effort is learned from past value, so a gate should be learned from logged outcomes (our own runs) rather than set by hand.

source: Callaway, Rangel, Griffiths (2021) Fixation patterns in simple choice reflect optimal information sampling
finding: Models where people look in value-based choice as an optimal metalevel MDP: sample from options whose value estimates are both high and uncertain. Fits a binary and a trinary snack-choice dataset.
numbers: Five free parameters (sample noise, cost per sample, cost of switching attention, prior bias, softmax temperature); one set fit on even trials of both datasets; 70 snacks rated, 100 choices per person, 50 Hz gaze. Fixation time follows relative rating in the trinary but not the binary case, as the model predicts.
limits: Compared with attentional drift diffusion; fit statistics not extracted. Rating is a proxy for the internal value estimate.
agent_relevance: VOC-style sampling logic fits behaviour at the fixation level, not only at the task level.

source: Authors not checked (2025, Cognitive Science) Time Spent Thinking in Online Chess Reflects the Value of Computation
finding: Natural-data test of VOC in humans. In over 12 million online chess games, move time rises with the estimated benefit of deeper search (Stockfish deep value versus depth-1 value). The link is stronger in higher-Elo players and when the benefit is estimated only from what the player could know.
numbers: Over 12 million games. Elo-by-benefit interaction estimates range 0.02 to 3.07 across time-control settings, all p below 1e-50; authors call the Elo effect significant and robust but modest. Relationship is concave and grows with total time and increment. Move time rises with expected benefit even when the true benefit is 0.
limits: Observational. Stockfish depth-1 stands in for play without computation. Modest effect. A cost-of-time model explains only qualitative features.
agent_relevance: Stronger players tie thinking time to value more tightly, so a gate is a skill. Expected benefit predicts effort even when real benefit is nil, so a gate can be fooled by surface cues.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning
finding: Psychological Review. Proposes that people pick among cognitive strategies by trading expected accuracy against time cost. Known to me from memory and the citing papers only.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Memory only; needs a source check before use.
agent_relevance: Human parallel for choosing which operator to try next (O1-O8).

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Hsu (2018) Overrepresentation of extreme events in decision making reflects rational use of cognitive resources
finding: Psychological Review. Rational-resource account of why extreme outcomes are over-weighted. Seen only in a Europe PMC listing; full text did not load.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Title and year from a search listing.
agent_relevance: Biases as optimal use of few samples. Weak link to our work.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources
finding: Behavioral and Brain Sciences. Method: derive the best algorithm under cost limits, then test it against data. Cited by the chess paper (a22) as the programme behind these models.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Memory and citing papers only.
agent_relevance: Method template: define cost, derive policy, compare against a plain model (matches G7).

source: Callaway et al. (2022) Rational use of cognitive resources in human planning
finding: Nature Human Behaviour. Reported to show that human planning strategies match a policy derived from a metalevel MDP. Listed in Europe PMC; paywalled.
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Nature page redirected to a login wall; a preprint version was not fetched.
agent_relevance: Strongest human test of VOC-based planning; read before any claim of human fit.

source: Horvitz (1987/1990) Computation and action under bounded resources; Matheson (1968) The economic value of analysis and computation
finding: Early lines of the value-of-computation idea: Matheson tied computation to information value; Horvitz built the expected-value-of-computation view. Both named in Hay et al. (a02) as precursors.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Named only in the text of Hay et al. (2012).
agent_relevance: The idea is about 50 years older than LLMs and has a stable theory base.

source: Gap note across angle-A sources
finding: No source read here tests a VOC gate on an agent with tools or on open-ended tasks without a checkable answer. RaM, Arora, Chen, AdaptThink and Thinkless all train weights; none works at prompt level only. Adaptive-Consistency is the one inference-time method.
numbers: All trained LLM results are on maths or multiple-choice benchmarks.
limits: Absence in the sources read; not proof of absence in the literature. Web search quota was exhausted this session and the arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited, so forward-citation search was limited.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold has to test its own S0/S6 gate (G7); no paper does it for us.
